questions.q: A stationary source emits sound of frequency 500 Hz. An observer moves toward the source at 20 m/s. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the observed frequency? Write the formula you use and identify each variable with its sign.
questions.a: Formula: \(f' = f \frac{v + v_o}{v}\) (observer moving toward stationary source). Given: \(f = 500 \text{ Hz}\), \(v = 340 \text{ m/s}\), \(v_o = +20 \text{ m/s}\) (toward source). \(f' = 500 \times \frac{340 + 20}{340} = 500 \times \frac{360}{340} \approx 529.4 \text{ Hz}\). A wrong answer (e.g., 470 Hz) reveals the student used the wrong sign for \(v_o\) or confused the formula with the source-moving case \(f' = f \frac{v}{v - v_s}\).

questions.q: Explain why the Doppler shift for a source moving toward a stationary observer at speed \(v_s\) is \(f' = f \frac{v}{v - v_s}\), while for an observer moving toward a stationary source at the same speed \(v_o = v_s\), the shift is \(f' = f \frac{v + v_o}{v}\). Why are these two expressions not equal even though the relative speed is the same?
questions.a: Sound requires a medium; the wave speed \(v\) is defined relative to the medium. When the source moves, it compresses wavefronts in the medium, altering the wavelength \(\lambda' = \frac{v - v_s}{f}\). The observer receives these shortened waves at speed \(v\), so \(f' = \frac{v}{\lambda'} = f \frac{v}{v - v_s}\). When the observer moves, the wavelength in the medium is unchanged (\(\lambda = v/f\)), but the observer encounters wavefronts at relative speed \(v + v_o\), giving \(f' = \frac{v + v_o}{\lambda} = f \frac{v + v_o}{v}\). The asymmetry arises because the medium breaks Galilean relativity for sound. A student who claims they are equal confuses sound with light (where no medium exists).

questions.q: A police car with a siren of frequency 800 Hz moves at 30 m/s toward a stationary observer. Simultaneously, the observer starts running toward the police car at 5 m/s. Speed of sound = 330 m/s. Calculate the observed frequency. Show all steps with units.
questions.a:
Step 1: Identify given: \(f = 800 \text{ Hz}\), \(v = 330 \text{ m/s}\), \(v_s = +30 \text{ m/s}\) (source toward observer), \(v_o = +5 \text{ m/s}\) (observer toward source).
Step 2: Formula for both moving toward each other: \(f' = f \frac{v + v_o}{v - v_s}\).
Step 3: Substitute: \(f' = 800 \times \frac{330 + 5}{330 - 30} = 800 \times \frac{335}{300}\).
Step 4: Compute: \(\frac{335}{300} = 1.1167\), \(f' = 800 \times 1.1167 = 893.3 \text{ Hz}\).
Step 5: Check: Both motions increase frequency, so \(f' > 800 \text{ Hz}\) — physically reasonable. A wrong answer like 853 Hz suggests using \(f' = f \frac{v}{v - v_s}\) (ignoring observer motion) or sign error in \(v_o\).

questions.q: Two cars A and B move on a straight road. Car A (source) emits a horn at 440 Hz and moves at 25 m/s. Car B (observer) moves at 15 m/s. Speed of sound = 340 m/s. Calculate the observed frequency in four cases: (a) both moving toward each other, (b) both moving away from each other, (c) A chasing B (same direction, A behind), (d) B chasing A (same direction, B behind). Tabulate your results and explain the trend.
questions.a:
(a) Toward: \(f' = 440 \times \frac{340 + 15}{340 - 25} = 440 \times \frac{355}{315} = 495.9 \text{ Hz}\).
(b) Away: \(f' = 440 \times \frac{340 - 15}{340 + 25} = 440 \times \frac{325}{365} = 391.8 \text{ Hz}\).
(c) A chases B: relative motion = A approaches B from behind. \(v_s = +25\), \(v_o = +15\) (both in same direction, but A catches up). Sign convention: if both move right, and A is behind B, A moves toward B (+\(v_s\)), B moves away from A (-\(v_o\) relative to source direction). Correct: source toward observer (+\(v_s\)), observer away from source (-\(v_o\)). \(f' = 440 \times \frac{340 - 15}{340 - 25} = 440 \times \frac{325}{315} = 454.0 \text{ Hz}\).
(d) B chases A: source away from observer (-\(v_s\)), observer toward source (+\(v_o\)). \(f' = 440 \times \frac{340 + 15}{340 + 25} = 440 \times \frac{355}{365} = 428.0 \text{ Hz}\).
Trend: Highest when approaching head-on, lowest when receding head-on. Chasing cases give intermediate shifts. Wrong signs in chasing cases are the most common error — students must define positive direction consistently.

questions.q: A student solves a Doppler problem: "Source frequency 600 Hz, source speed 40 m/s toward observer, observer speed 10 m/s away from source, sound speed 330 m/s." The student writes \(f' = 600 \times \frac{330 - 10}{330 - 40} = 600 \times \frac{320}{290} = 662 \text{ Hz}\). Identify the error, correct it, and explain why the student's reasoning was flawed.
questions.a: Error: Sign of \(v_s\). Source moves TOWARD observer, so \(v_s = +40 \text{ m/s}\) (denominator \(v - v_s\)). Observer moves AWAY from source, so \(v_o = -10 \text{ m/s}\) (numerator \(v + v_o = v - 10\)). Student used \(v - v_s\) correctly but should have used \(v - 10\) in numerator. Correct: \(f' = 600 \times \frac{330 - 10}{330 - 40} = 600 \times \frac{320}{290} = 662 \text{ Hz}\) — wait, the student's numerical answer is accidentally correct because both signs were wrong in a compensating way! The student likely thinks "toward = minus in denominator, away = minus in numerator" as a memorized rule without understanding. The flaw: they don't grasp that the formula \(f' = f \frac{v + v_o}{v - v_s}\) uses a SINGLE sign convention: \(v_o\) positive if observer moves TOWARD source, \(v_s\) positive if source moves TOWARD observer. Here \(v_o = -10\), \(v_s = +40\). The student's answer is numerically correct but conceptually wrong — they would fail if both moved toward (\(v_o = +10, v_s = +40\)) and they'd write \(\frac{330 - 10}{330 - 40}\) instead of \(\frac{330 + 10}{330 - 40}\).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a smartphone and a Bluetooth speaker to measure the speed of sound using the Doppler Effect. Describe the procedure, measurements needed, and the formula you would use to calculate \(v\). Assume you can measure frequency accurately using a spectrum analyzer app.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Fix a Bluetooth speaker on a toy car moving at constant known speed \(v_s\) (measure with stopwatch and meter tape). (2) Speaker plays a pure tone of known frequency \(f\) (e.g., 1000 Hz from a signal generator app). (3) Smartphone with spectrum analyzer app acts as stationary observer at a fixed position on the car's path. (4) Record the frequency \(f'\) when the car approaches directly toward the phone. (5) Use formula \(f' = f \frac{v}{v - v_s}\) (observer stationary, source moving toward). Solve for \(v\): \(v = \frac{f' v_s}{f' - f}\). (6) Repeat for receding case \(f'' = f \frac{v}{v + v_s}\) for verification. Key requirement: car speed \(v_s\) must be known independently (not from Doppler shift). A poor answer would suggest using the phone as both source and observer (circular) or ignoring the need to know \(v_s\) independently.
